content.text:
### Type-safe query with row type interface

Source: https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/v3.4.5/deno/README.md

Define a TypeScript interface for row data and pass it as a generic to the sql tag to get type-safe results. Accessing properties not defined on the interface will cause a type error.

```TypeScript
interface User {
  id: number
  name: string
}

const users = await sql<User[]>`SELECT * FROM users`
users[0].id // ok => number
users[1].name // ok => string
users[0].invalid // fails: `invalid` does not exists on `User`
```

--------------------------------

### TypeScript support

Source: https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/v3.4.5/deno/README.md

`postgres` has TypeScript support. You can pass a row list type for your queries in this way:
```ts
interface User {
  id: number
  name: string
}

const users = await sql<User[]>`SELECT * FROM users`
users[0].id // ok => number
users[1].name // ok => string
users[0].invalid // fails: `invalid` does not exists on `User`
```

However, be sure to check the array length to avoid accessing properties of `undefined` rows:
```ts
const users = await sql<User[]>`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`
if (!users.length)
  throw new Error('Not found')
return users[0]
```

You can also prefer destructuring when you only care about a fixed number of rows.
In this case, we recommend you to prefer using tuples to handle `undefined` properly:
```ts
const [user]: [User?] = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`
if (!user) // => User | undefined
  throw new Error('Not found')
return user // => User

// NOTE:
const [first, second]: [User?] = await sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` // fails: `second` does not exist on `[User?]`
const [first, second] = await sql<[User?]>`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` // don't fail : `second: User | undefined`
```

We do our best to type all the public API, however types are not always updated when features are added or changed. Feel free to open an issue if you have trouble with types.

--------------------------------

### Numbers, bigint, numeric

Source: https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/v3.4.5/README.md

`Number` in javascript is only able to represent 2<sup>53</sup>-1 safely which means that types in PostgreSQLs like `bigint` and `numeric` won't fit into `Number`.

Since Node.js v10.4 we can use [`BigInt`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/BigInt) to match the PostgreSQL type `bigint` which is returned for eg. `count(*)`. Unfortunately, it doesn't work with `JSON.stringify` out of the box, so Postgres.js will return it as a string.

If you want to use `BigInt` you can add this custom type:

```js
const sql = postgres({
  types: {
    bigint: postgres.BigInt
  }
})
```

There is currently no guaranteed way to handle `numeric` / `decimal` types in native Javascript. **These [and similar] types will be returned as a `string`**. The best way in this case is to use  [custom types](#custom-types).

--------------------------------

### Custom Type: bigint

Source: https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/v3.4.5/README.md

Configure Postgres.js to use BigInt for PostgreSQL bigint columns. This custom type can be added via the types option when creating a postgres client.

```APIDOC

### Description
Configure Postgres.js to use BigInt for PostgreSQL bigint columns. This custom type can be added via the types option when creating a postgres client.

### Method
N/A (Configuration)

### Endpoint
N/A

### Parameters
#### Configuration
- **types** (object) - Required - An object mapping PostgreSQL type names to custom type handlers.
  - **bigint** (function) - Required - The `postgres.BigInt` handler to use for bigint columns.

### Response
N/A

### Request Example
```js
const sql = postgres({
  types: {
    bigint: postgres.BigInt
  }
})
```
```

--------------------------------

Source: https://github.com/porsager/postgres/blob/v3.4.5/deno/README.md

Shows how to configure Postgres.js to return bigint values as JavaScript BigInt instead of strings.

I added tags, and `npm run check` passes. I didn't run the migration or the query against a database.

- **`migrations/002_tags.sql`**: adds a `tags` table with a unique `name`. It also adds a `bookmark_tags` join table, which is what lets a bookmark have many tags and a tag sit on many bookmarks. Deleting a bookmark or a tag removes its join rows. There's an index on `tag_id` for the count query and later tag lookups.
- **`src/tags.ts`**: `listTags()` returns each tag's `id`, `name` and `bookmark_count`, with the most-used tags first and ties broken by name. Tags with no bookmarks show up with a count of 0.

I checked the postgres.js 3.4.5 docs through context7. `count()` returns a bigint, which postgres.js hands back as a string. The query casts it with `::int` so `bookmark_count` is a number. The `id` field is still a string in `TagCount`, because `id` is a `BIGSERIAL`.

There's no function yet to create tags or attach them to bookmarks. I held back because you only asked for the schema and the listing, and tags come next. I can add those if you want.
